desc: Short for Positive Mental Attitude, the philosophy championed by KEMURI. Widely known as a symbol of Japanese ska punk.
Music born in Jamaica, characterized by an offbeat rhythm. In Japan, artists like MUTE BEAT, Tokyo Ska Paradise Orchestra, and KEMURI fused it with dub and punk.
The trend by which original Japanese-language folk spread nationwide, connecting to the singer-songwriter culture of artists like Takuro Yoshida and Yosui Inoue.

A movement in which young people in the Kansai region sang about society and everyday life in their own words during the late 1960s. Key figures include Nobuyasu Okabayashi, Tomoya Takaishi, and Goro Nakagawa.
Music built on the form of American blues, sung in Japanese and regional dialects about the reality of urban life. Deeply intersects with kayokyoku, folk, and rock.
A uniquely Japanese blues culture cultivated in 1970s Osaka, Kyoto, and Kobe by artists like Yuka Dan, West Road Blues Band, and Masaki Ueda.
Japanese popular song that developed around records, radio, and television during the Shōwa era. Spans a wide range, from enka to pop.
A term for the polished, singer-songwriter-centered pop that branched off from folk starting in the 1970s.
A retrospective term for urbane Japanese pop of the 1970s–80s. Its rediscovery overseas has been significant.
Pop music that actively used synthesizers and sequencers. The emergence of YMO is emblematic.
The phenomenon of a wave of young bands emerging through TV shows and pedestrian-precinct street performances (hokoten) from the late 1980s into the early 1990s.
A culture originating in Japan that unites costume, makeup, and stage performance with rock. Not confined to a single musical genre.
A pop movement of the 1990s that drew on Shibuya's record-shop culture, crossing soft rock, bossa nova, and more.
A collective term for the artists whose songs Tetsuya Komuro wrote, composed, and produced in the 1990s.
A name for Japanese popular music that took hold from the late 1980s. Its use on the radio station J-WAVE is considered the trigger for its spread.
A creative culture built on voice-synthesis software and video-sharing sites, flexibly connecting creators and singers.
Performers who primarily sing and post covers of existing songs or Vocaloid songs on video sites. Has also sent talent into today's pop scene.
An era in which songs are primarily heard through subscription streaming. Hits are now more likely to emerge from playlists and social media.
